text: William Francis Carrigan (October 22, 1883 – July 8, 1969), nicknamed "Rough," was an American Major League baseball catcher and manager. He played for the Boston Red Sox from 1906 to 1916, serving as a player-manager for the last four of those seasons. In 1915 and 1916, Carrigan's teams won back-to-back World Series, and he compiled an 8–2 record as a manager in World Series play, achieving the highest postseason winning percentage (.800) among managers with multiple postseason appearances. He was recognized with a spot on the Honor Rolls of Baseball in 1946. Carrigan was known for combining toughness with intelligence and had a close relationship with Red Sox star Babe Ruth, serving as his roommate and manager; Ruth referred to Carrigan as the best manager he ever played for and described him as a combination father, confessor, drill sergeant, psychologist, and Dutch uncle. Carrigan also maintained a friendly relationship with Detroit Tigers star Ty Cobb, both of whom were known for their intense play. A religious schism among Red Sox players and coaches in the early 1910s led to Carrigan being appointed player-manager in 1913 after team co-owner Jimmy McAleer fired Stahl, following a fistfight between Speaker and Carrigan in which Carrigan won. The Red Sox finished second in 1914 and paid $25,000 to Baltimore of the International League for Babe Ruth, Ernie Shore, and Ben Egan; Ruth gave up 21 hits in 23 innings pitched that year. Before the 1915 season, Carrigan received a dispensation from the Catholic Church to marry Protestant woman Beulah Bartlett, a childhood friend. He led the Red Sox to World Series titles in 1915 and 1916, making him the only manager to win two World Series titles with Boston until Terry Francona achieved the feat in 2007. In August 1916, Carrigan discussed retiring with Red Sox owner Joseph Lannin due to family obligations and a desire to reduce travel time and focus on his theater business, the Maine and New Hampshire Theater Corporation, which owned up to fifty theaters and included partners William P. Gray, Albert Hyslop, and John H. Bartlett. He sold his shares in the corporation to Gray in January 1922 for between $200,000 and $250,000. Rumors circulated after his departure about a return to baseball, including speculation he might buy the Red Sox from Harry Frazee, but he returned as manager in 1927, leading the team to last place in each of three consecutive seasons. In early December 1929, Carrigan hesitated about accepting President Bob Quinn's offer to return as manager, and he ultimately resigned on December 20. From 1933 to 1934, he served as head baseball coach at Bates College. In 1953, he became president of People's Savings Bank in Lewiston, and his wife died in 1958. Carrigan died at Central Maine General Hospital in Lewiston at age 85 and was posthumously elected to the Boston Red Sox Hall of Fame in 2004. He was born in Lewiston, Maine, and played football and baseball at Lewiston High School, also playing roller polo, which led to fights and prompted his brother to stop it. He studied at the College of the Holy Cross in Worcester, Massachusetts, a school known for sending its baseball players to the major leagues. Carrigan's brother John was a talented pitcher, and Carrigan served as his catcher.
